body_markdown:
Budget season is here. And if your tech line item looks like a junk drawer of logins nobody remembers signing up for, you're in good company.


Property management teams have added a lot of tools over the past few years, including leasing platforms, resident apps, smart locks, AI chatbots, maintenance software, and reporting dashboards. Some of them have changed how your sites run, while others are quietly billing you every month for features your team stopped using last spring.


The fix isn't a bigger budget. It's a sharper one. Before you sign another renewal, sort every tool into one of three buckets:


**Keep, Cut, or Pilot.**


##


**Your 2027 Tech Budget**


###


**Keep: The Tools That Pull Their Weight**


These are the tools your team would fight you to hang on to. They save real hours, connect to your core systems, and residents actually notice them.


A tool belongs in the Keep pile when:


-


Your onsite team uses it every day without being reminded


-


You can point to a clear result, like faster work order turns, fewer missed tours, or shorter vacancy windows


-


It plays nicely with your property management system instead of creating double entry


-


Residents or tenants would notice (and complain) if it disappeared


But keeping a tool doesn't mean ignoring it. Use renewal time to renegotiate pricing, trim unused seats, and ask the vendor what's on their 2027 roadmap.


###


**Cut: The Tools That Cost More Than They Give**


Here's where the savings live. Every portfolio has a few subscriptions that made sense once and don't anymore.


A tool belongs in the Cut pile when:


-


Fewer than half the people with a license actually log in


-


It overlaps with something you already pay for


-


Your team has built workarounds (hello, shared spreadsheets) to avoid it


-


Nobody can explain what it does in one sentence


Cutting feels risky, but it's usually the opposite. Fewer tools means less training, fewer passwords, and a cleaner picture of your data. Give your team a heads-up, export what you need, and set a firm sunset date.


###


**Pilot: The Tools Worth a Real Test**


This is the fun bucket with AI leasing assistants, predictive maintenance, smarter rent pricing, and automated resident communication. There's a lot of promise out there, and a lot of hype too.


The trick is to test small before you commit. A good pilot has:


-


**One clear goal:** "Cut lead response time in half" beats "see if AI helps."


-


**A short window:** Sixty to ninety days is enough to get an impression of support.


-


**A limited footprint:** Start with a few properties, not the whole portfolio.


-


**A named owner:** Someone onsite who will give honest feedback, both good and bad.


-


**A decision date:** When the pilot ends, it moves to Keep or Cut. No excuses.


Set aside a slice of your 2027 tech budget just for pilots. That way you can say yes to smart experiments without blowing up the plan.


##


**Don't Forget the People Side**


Here's the part most tech budgets miss: software doesn't run your properties.


[People do.](https://www.bgsf.com/post/the-human-side-of-a-successful-go-live)


The best platform in the world won't move the needle if your leasing team is stretched thin or your maintenance crew never got trained on the new app. Rollouts take time. Pilots need someone with bandwidth to test them properly. And when a tool automates part of a role, that person's skills should shift toward the work only humans can do, like building resident relationships and solving tricky problems on the spot.


So as you build your budget, ask two questions for every tool:


1.


Who will use this every day?


2.


Do they have the time and training to use it well?


If the answer to the second one is "not really," then plan for it. That might mean building training into the rollout, or bringing in experienced temporary help to keep your sites covered while your core team learns the ropes.


##


**Make 2027 the Year Your Tech Stack Makes Sense**


A great tech budget isn't about having the most tools. It's about having the right ones, used by a team that's set up to win. So grab that list of subscriptions, gather your site leaders, and start sorting. Keep what works. Cut what doesn't. Pilot what might.
